title: Drummer friend Charles Meriwether and Chicago-style records
summary: Talk of a talented drummer friend, Charles Meriwether, who quit music; listening to Dodds and Ladnier records and a television show with Bud Freeman and Pee Wee Russell.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: He was able to play with a band within two weeks or something like that, wasn't he?
Yes, Arlen's very talented. There was no two ways about that. He's proven that I guess.
I mean he never got to be a professional quality, but it was just like that. It was fantastic. Who was your friend that was a drummer?

That boy later turned out, I think he's kind of an unprofessional beatnik right now. He is very talented. He painted very well. And I understand he's writing very well, but he kind of lost interest in music completely because modern jazz confused him, although he liked it very much. I think he came to the same realization that I did, that you had to play music, the music that was expressive of your time, if it was to be improvisation anyway. What's his name? His name was Charles Meriwether. Actually I was always instigating him into these things and he was kind of a reluctant partner to these things. He had a very natural talent. I remember him playing things. He had a natural feeling for the beginning of choruses, the beginning and ending of choruses. In other words a natural meter, which very few people had, even musicians. He didn't have to be seen, well this is the bridge of the tune and here you play something to introduce the bridge of the tune. He didn't have to be shown any of these things. He did all these things very naturally. And it was quite, to me I was very impressed with it. But he's very unconscious of the fact that he had this, you know, he had this thing going. And he just fell away from music completely. We used to get together a whole lot and listen to Dodds, the records Dodds made, you know, Dodds washboard things. And he was a great admirer of the trombonist. And the guy that made those things with Jelly played very well as I remember. And also Tommy Ladnier, who used to dig Tommy Ladnier a lot. And I never went through the Chicago school stage, you know, too much. I dug some of the things that were going on. But not too much. I can see it, you know, as a valid musical form, especially now. I think actually they're playing, from what I've heard of them lately, they're playing better now than they ever did. I saw a television show with Bud Freeman, Pee Wee Russell, and Bob Hackett playing bass. The only thing that was missing was Wettling. I was kind of disappointed that they had Kruper in his place. But it's very valid, very groovy. I should have liked it a lot more.
